summary: Oral ketotifen (ketotifen fumarate) is a second-generation H1-antihistamine that also has mast-cell stabilizing activity, used for the prophylaxis of bronchial asthma and the symptomatic treatment of allergic conditions including allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis and atopic disorders. As an asthma prophylactic it is not a bronchodilator and does not relieve acute attacks; the full anti-asthmatic effect may take several weeks to develop, and existing anti-asthma therapy should not be stopped abruptly when ketotifen is started. Compared with non-sedating antihistamines it more commonly causes sedation/drowsiness and weight gain, especially early in treatment. Standard adult and child (>3 years) dosing is 1 mg twice daily with food, increasing to 2 mg twice daily if needed, to a maximum of 4 mg/day. Oral ketotifen is NOT FDA-approved in the US (only the ophthalmic eye-drop form is marketed there); this record is based on the EMA/Zaditen SmPC and BNF rather than an openFDA label.

moa: Ketotifen is a non-competitive antagonist of the histamine H1 receptor and also stabilizes mast cells, inhibiting the release and activity of mediators of allergic and inflammatory reactions (histamine, leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor). It additionally inhibits accumulation of eosinophils and attenuates the development of airway hyperreactivity, which underlies its prophylactic (rather than bronchodilator) effect in asthma. Central H1 blockade accounts for its sedative effect, more pronounced than with non-sedating second-generation agents.

preg: There is limited experience with ketotifen in pregnancy; avoid use during pregnancy unless clearly necessary and the expected benefit outweighs potential risk (EMA/SmPC).
lact: Although animal data suggest excretion into milk, human data are limited; because of the potential for sedation and anticholinergic effects in the infant, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment unless considered essential.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is established in the SmPC; use with caution and monitor for exaggerated CNS effects in significant impairment.
hepatic: Ketotifen is extensively metabolized by the liver; use with caution in hepatic impairment as exposure and sedative effects may be increased.

pearls: ORAL ketotifen is NOT FDA-approved in the US - only the ophthalmic (eye-drop) form is US-marketed; this record is based on the EMA/Zaditen SmPC and BNF rather than an openFDA label
It is a prophylactic agent in asthma, NOT a bronchodilator - it does not treat acute attacks and full effect takes weeks
Do not stop existing anti-asthma therapy abruptly when starting ketotifen; withdraw other agents only gradually under supervision
More sedating than non-sedating second-generation antihistamines; weight gain/increased appetite is also notable
Watch for reversible thrombocytopenia when combined with oral antidiabetic drugs - monitor platelet count
Starting with a lower evening dose can reduce initial daytime drowsiness
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember with food; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual twice-daily schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up.
overdose: Overdose features include drowsiness, confusion, disorientation, tachycardia and hypotension, and in children CNS excitation, hyperexcitability or convulsions. There is no specific antidote; manage symptomatically and supportively with attention to airway, breathing and circulation. Consider activated charcoal and gastric emptying if presentation is recent; control seizures with benzodiazepines and monitor cardiovascular status.
